stories.title: FADU Unveils AI Data Center-Focused Vision at 2026 OCP Korea Tech Day
stories.summary: South Korean SSD controller maker FADU presented its AI data center-focused technology vision at the 2026 OCP Korea Tech Day event. The company outlined how its storage and controller technologies target the demands of AI-era data center infrastructure.
stories.why_it_matters: FADU's pitch reflects how component-level suppliers are repositioning around AI workloads, where storage throughput and efficiency have become bottlenecks. Its presence at an OCP event also underscores open-hardware standards gaining traction in Korea, giving local chipmakers a channel into hyperscale and AI infrastructure supply chains traditionally dominated by larger global players.
stories.content:
## Presentation of Key Challenges for Flash Memory and SSDs  

Full-scale Launch of the 'FADU 2.0' Vision

    FADU, a specialist in data center semiconductors, announced on the 24th that it unveiled its storage vision optimized for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers at the '2026 OCP Korea Tech Day' held at COEX in Seoul on the 21st.

On the 21st, visitors at the ‘2026 OCP Korea Tech Day’ held at COEX in Seoul listen to an explanation about Fadu Gen6 technology. Fadu

View original image
The OCP Korea Tech Day is an official annual conference that has been organized by the Open Compute Project (OCP) Foundation and the OCP Korea Community since 2019, bringing together hyperscalers (large-scale data center operators), leading semiconductor companies, infrastructure suppliers, and startups from around the world.

At this year’s event, which drew around 1,500 attendees, FADU’s Dr. Seungmin Kim delivered a keynote speech entitled "Flash Memory in AI Data Centers: The New Role of SSDs and Controllers." Dr. Kim explained that as explosive data growth and cost efficiency emerge as key challenges in the era of AI, the role of SSDs is becoming more specialized in terms of memory, performance, and capacity units. He identified four key challenges that SSDs need to address: ▲small input/output (I/O) unit processing performance ▲consistent latency ▲GPU-driven I/O ▲line-rate security.

FADU set up a large exhibition booth at the event to showcase its next-generation Gen6 SSD solutions and other major products and technologies. This exhibition is part of the 'FADU 2.0' vision, which was recently announced at 'FMS 2026', the largest memory event in North America. Rather than focusing solely on a single controller, the company’s strategy is to expand its portfolio to offer broad data center solutions to meet growing AI demand. In particular, FADU revealed a bold plan to drive innovation not only in areas such as research and development, but also across the entire organization as it evolves toward the 'FADU 2.0 vision.'

stories.title: S-Energy Expands into AI Data Center O&M with 3 Billion Won Annual Revenue Deal
stories.summary: South Korea's S-Energy has signed a deal to expand into AI data center operations and maintenance services. The contract is expected to generate stable annual revenue of about 3 billion won over a five-year period.
stories.why_it_matters: The deal shows how the AI data center boom is creating adjacent revenue streams beyond construction, pulling in companies from adjacent sectors like energy equipment into long-term O&M contracts. For S-Energy, it diversifies income with multi-year recurring revenue; for the market, it signals that Korea's AI infrastructure buildout is maturing into an operational phase that sustains a services ecosystem.
stories.content:
![\[Click eStock\] "S-Energy Expands into AI Data Center O&M...Stable Annual Revenue of 3 Billion Won for 5 Years"](https://cphoto.asiae.co.kr/listimglink/1/2026081918500185686_1787133001.jpg) View original image

S-Energy, a company specializing in solar power, is expanding its business scope beyond engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) of solar projects to include energy operation and maintenance (O&M) services for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers in the Asia-Pacific region.

On August 24, independent research firm ValueFinder analyzed that S-Energy has secured an annual average of about 3 billion won in ESG operation and maintenance contracts over five years by joining the Singapore-led Asia-Pacific hyperscale AI data center project as an investor.

Founded in 2001, S-Energy is a solar power specialist that was listed on KOSDAQ in 2007. Its main business areas are manufacturing solar cell modules and developing solar power generation systems, and it has continued to expand its domestic and international solar power operations.

Recently, S-Energy has been fostering AI data centers as its next-generation growth business. In collaboration with the Ministry of Climate and Environment’s “Green Infrastructure Global Export Support Fund II,” S-Energy participated in a hyperscale AI data center project in the Asia-Pacific region led by a Singapore digital infrastructure developer.

The total project investment is 22.1 million dollars, or approximately 3.15 billion won, combining the fund and S-Energy's capital. S-Energy has gone beyond simple investment by also securing the ESG operation and maintenance business for this project. The contract duration is five years, with expected annual operational revenue of around 3 billion won.

ValueFinder evaluated that this contract marks a shift from S-Energy’s previous EPC-focused business structure to an energy service business generating recurring operational revenue.

ValueFinder researcher Jihoo commented, “This O&M contract is significant not only for expanding beyond simple solar EPC sales, but also for securing a stable recurring revenue source in the AI data center segment.”

S-Energy is reported to have a pipeline for hyperscale AI data center development in the Asia-Pacific region, including Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan. It is also analyzed that, as data center projects begin in earnest, the company may win additional contracts for energy operation and maintenance services.

S-Energy’s overseas solar projects are also progressing. On August 11, S-Energy’s Japan subsidiary signed a turnkey contract for the ‘Tojo Megasolar Farm’ repowering project in Hiroshima Prefecture, Japan. The contract is valued at approximately 7.2 hundred million won.

This project involves replacing the existing modules of a 33-megawatt-class extra-high-voltage solar power plant (based on direct current). The contract counterparty is Kameda, a prime market-listed company in Japan.

In addition, S-Energy is expanding its overseas business with projects such as the repowering of Yotsukaido No.1 Solar Power Plant in Japan and supplying solar modules based on heterojunction technology (HJT) to the Middle East.

In Korea, S-Energy is carrying out various projects, such as supplying high-efficiency modules for the Namdong National Industrial Complex in Incheon and supplying building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) for the Seoul Arena cultural complex. The company has also been selected as the principal organization for a government-backed offshore solar power module development and demonstration project, securing technology for large-scale renewable energy projects like Saemangeum.

ValueFinder noted that S-Energy is expanding into the AI data center energy business by leveraging its accumulated EPC and operational management capabilities from its existing solar business.

stories.title: Debt-Laden Guizhou Hosts Some of China's Biggest Data Centers
stories.summary: China's Guizhou province, one of the country's most indebted regions, has become home to some of China's largest data centers. The province has leveraged its cool climate and cheap energy to attract major cloud and computing investments despite its strained public finances.
stories.why_it_matters: The story highlights a growing tension in China's digital infrastructure strategy: capital-intensive data center buildouts are being concentrated in fiscally fragile regions, raising questions about who ultimately bears the cost if local government debt problems deepen. Operators and investors with exposure to Guizhou-based facilities face potential policy and financing risks, while the central government's data-localization push keeps demand anchored there regardless.
stories.content:
While the West fights data centers, Chinese villages welcome them

- **China is moving its AI data centers into poor rural provinces**
- **Guizhou offers cooler weather, cheap land, and abundant renewable power**
- **New data centers must draw 80% of power from renewables**

China is significantly expanding its data center capacity as artificial intelligence processing drives an unprecedented demand for computing power nationwide.

Much of this new infrastructure is being built away from the crowded eastern seaboard and placed in rural western provinces.

In 2021, the Chinese government formally named this approach the Eastern Data Western Computing strategy, marking a clear national policy shift.

## Why the rural west has the advantage

Provinces such as Guizhou and Inner Mongolia offer cooler climates, abundant renewable energy, and vast amounts of empty, affordable land.

China has also mandated that all new data centers draw 80% of their power from renewable sources before the decade ends.

Regions with expanded solar and wind capacity, like Guizhou, make it easier for operators to meet those goals, according to Rystad Energy analyst Simeng Deng.

Large-scale server farms can also absorb curtailed renewable output, easing the ongoing problem of overproduced solar and wind energy nationwide.

Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!

Developing previously overlooked rural regions has become another expected benefit, though researchers remain sharply divided on its actual economic impact.

## An uneven economic payoff

According to Andrew Stokols of Singapore Management University, data centers do not necessarily generate a meaningful ripple effect for local employment.

This pattern shows in Guizhou's growth figures, where heavy data center investment helped drive average annual GDP growth of 7.4% over the past decade, yet wage growth over that same period ranked second to last among all Chinese provinces, according to Taiwan-based researchers at DSET.

The province also carries one of China's heaviest public debt burdens, driven largely by heavy infrastructure spending and incentive programs.

In 2024, Guizhou also ranked 30th nationally for its debt-to-revenue ratio and 27th nationally for its debt-to-GDP ratio.

Still, residents of Guian New Area, a Guizhou district built around Huawei's largest data center, describe visible local change, including new roads, growing trade, and steady new job opportunities for residents living close by today as well.

Two universities have reportedly opened in the area since the data centers were constructed, according to local vendors.

Despite this uneven mix of growth, debt, and stalled wages, fierce global competition over computing power keeps construction of new facilities moving steadily forward.

China is expected to nearly double its total data center capacity within the next five years, industry estimates suggest, momentum which shows why Chinese policy documents were already linking computing power to national strength, even before AI's rapid growth.

"It's essential for national competitiveness in the age of digital technology," said Stokols.

Unlike in Europe and the United States, where data center projects often face local resistance, dissent in China remains tightly controlled.

The pattern suggests China is treating computing infrastructure as a matter of national strategy rather than pure local economic development.

Whether rural provinces eventually see the broader prosperity officials have long promised remains, for now, an open and unresolved question.

Via Techxplore

stories.title: Singapore Launches Data Center Powered by Human Neurons
stories.summary: Singapore has launched a data center powered by human neurons, according to a report. The facility represents an experimental approach to computing using biological, brain-cell-based processing rather than conventional silicon hardware.
stories.why_it_matters: If accurate, this positions Singapore at the experimental frontier of biocomputing — a field that promises drastic energy efficiency gains over conventional AI hardware but remains unproven at scale. For a market that tightly rations data center capacity and power, hosting such pilots reinforces Singapore's strategy of staying relevant through R&D leadership even as it restricts conventional megawatt growth.
stories.content:
20 biological CL1 computers running on lab-grown neurons have been combined into a single server rack.

Developers in Singapore have launched a prototype of the world's first biological data center based on living human neurons. The project organizers grew biological cells from human stem cells in a laboratory at the medical faculty of the National University of Singapore, reports The Next Web.

The medical faculty of the National University of Singapore, data center operator DayOne, and Australian company Cortical Labs presented the equipment to a group of 80 guests on August 6, 2026. Engineers combined 20 CL1 computers into a single server rack.

Specialists from the Institute of Life Sciences grew living human cells from human stem cells. Each device contains biological processors and requires constant care to keep the neurons alive. Life support systems include pumps for delivering nutrients, temperature control, a gas mixture, and water filtration. The project's creators plan to carry out server maintenance once every six months.

The creators cite energy savings as the main advantage of biological computers. The entire biological rack consumes between 800 and 1,000 watts of power, which is comparable to running several home computers. Conventional silicon server racks for artificial intelligence operations require up to one hundred kilowatts of power.

The world's first CL1 biological computers went on sale as early as March 2, 2025. However, the emergence of this technology sparked serious ethical debates among scientists. Although the neurons in the CL1 are lab-grown and do not possess consciousness, this has provoked discussions about the nature of consciousness and the possibility of such biological systems experiencing suffering.

As the UOJ reported, a US startup will edit embryo genes.
